description: How magma viscosity controls eruption style and how lava flows, sills, dykes and plutons are identified.
content_html:
What Controls How a Volcano Erupts?

Not all volcanoes are the same. Some gently pour out thin lava flows that travel kilometres; others explode catastrophically, hurling ash and rock high into the atmosphere. The key variable is viscosity — how easily magma flows. Viscosity is controlled mainly by silica content and temperature. High-silica magmas (like those that feed andesite and rhyolite volcanoes) are sticky and trap dissolved gases; pressure builds until the eruption is explosive. Low-silica basaltic magmas are runny, allowing gases to escape gradually, producing quiet, passive eruptions.

Eruption Styles

A fissure eruption occurs when lava erupts through a linear crack in the crust rather than from a single point. The erupted lava is typically basaltic (low viscosity) and pours out in wide, flat sheets. Iceland is the best modern example, where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge intersects the island. Fissure eruptions produce broad lava plateaux and shield volcanoes with very gentle slopes.

A central vent eruption occurs when magma reaches the surface through a single pipe or chimney. The shape of the resulting volcano depends on magma viscosity. Basaltic magma builds a shield volcano with low, gently sloping sides because the lava flows far before solidifying. Higher-viscosity magma (andesitic) builds a steeper stratovolcano with more explosive eruptions and layers of ash and lava. Explosive eruptions can produce pyroclastic material — fragments of rock and solidified lava blown into the air.

Key Fact

High silica content = high viscosity = gases cannot escape = pressure builds = explosive eruption = steep-sided volcano. Low silica content = low viscosity = gases escape gradually = passive eruption = broad, gently sloping shield volcano.

Distinctive Lava Features

Basaltic lavas that cool slowly in thick flows often develop columnar jointing. As the lava cools and contracts, it cracks into regular polygonal columns, typically six-sided, perpendicular to the cooling surface. The Giant’s Causeway in Northern Ireland is the best-known British example. The columns are a direct record of the cooling geometry of the lava.

When basaltic lava erupts underwater, the outer surface quenches immediately in the cold seawater, forming rounded blobs known as pillow lava. Each new blob of lava breaks through the hardened skin of the previous one, producing a stack of overlapping pillows. Pillow lavas in the rock record are definitive evidence of submarine volcanic activity and are abundant in ancient ocean floor sequences preserved on land.

Key Fact

Columnar jointing — hexagonal columns in basalt, formed by contraction during cooling. Example: Giant’s Causeway, Northern Ireland. Pillow lava — rounded blobs formed when lava erupts underwater and quenches rapidly. Both are diagnostic field features used to interpret ancient volcanic environments.

Intrusive Igneous Bodies

Not all magma reaches the surface. Some cools and solidifies within the crust, forming intrusions. Three types are specified: sills, dykes and plutons. Each has a characteristic shape and field relationship that you need to recognise.

A sill is injected parallel to existing rock layers — it is concordant with the bedding. A sill can be recognised in the field because it lies parallel to the rock layers above and below it, and the rocks on both sides show baking (contact metamorphism) as evidence of heat. The Great Whin Sill of northern England is a well-known example, forming the resistant crag on which Hadrian’s Wall sits.

A dyke cuts across existing rock layers — it is discordant. Dykes are typically near-vertical and can be seen in coastal cliffs as dark sheets cross-cutting paler sedimentary beds. Because the dyke post-dates the rocks it cuts, cross-cutting relationships give relative age information: the dyke is always younger than the rocks it intrudes.

A pluton is a large, irregular igneous intrusion, typically of granitic composition. Plutons form deep in the crust where magma cools very slowly, producing the coarse grain size characteristic of granite. They often dome upwards, doming the overlying rocks. When erosion strips away the surrounding material over millions of years, the resistant granite is exposed at the surface. Dartmoor and Bodmin Moor in southwest England are parts of the Cornubian batholith — a chain of exposed granite plutons.

In the field, a pluton can be recognised by its lack of internal layering (unlike a sill), its irregular contact with surrounding country rock, and the metamorphic aureole — a zone of thermally altered rock surrounding the intrusion. The larger the pluton, the wider its aureole, because more heat was available over a longer cooling period.

The specification mentions a jelly lava flow simulation, which models how viscosity affects slope angle and flow shape. In the experiment, more viscous “lava” (thicker jelly) produces a steeper, shorter flow; less viscous “lava” (runnier jelly) spreads further and produces a shallower slope angle. This directly models the difference between a shield volcano built by low-viscosity basaltic lava and a steeper stratovolcano built by more viscous andesitic material. Exam questions may ask you to interpret the model or identify its limitations — for example, jelly does not reproduce temperature gradients or real gas behaviour.

Recognising intrusive and extrusive igneous bodies in the field and on geological maps is a core skill tested throughout the course. The field relationships — whether a body is concordant or discordant, whether it has a contact metamorphic aureole, and whether surrounding rocks are baked — are the primary evidence you will use when sequencing geological events in the next section on relative dating.
exam_tip_html: Questions on intrusive bodies often ask you to identify whether a feature is a sill or a dyke from a cross-section or map. The key rule: sills run parallel to bedding (concordant); dykes cut across bedding (discordant). For questions on volcanic eruption style, always link your answer back to silica content and viscosity — do not just state “it is more explosive” without explaining why. For the jelly experiment, state what the model shows (slope angle and flow distance as proxies for viscosity) and at least one limitation (does not model real temperature, pressure or gas escape). Slope angle comparison questions require you to state a measurement or comparative value, not just “one is steeper”.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Magma viscosity (controlled by silica content) determines eruption style: low viscosity = passive fissure or central vent eruptions building shield volcanoes; high viscosity = explosive eruptions building steeper stratovolcanoes.
  • Columnar jointing forms in thick basalt flows by contraction; pillow lava forms when basalt erupts underwater. Both are diagnostic field features for interpreting ancient volcanic environments.
  • Intrusive bodies: sills (concordant, parallel to bedding), dykes (discordant, cuts across bedding) and plutons (large, irregular, deep). Plutons are always younger than the rocks they intrude and older than any dykes or sills they feed.

practice_questions.text:
Which intrusive igneous body runs parallel to (concordant with) the surrounding rock layers?
A) Dyke
B) Pluton
C) Sill
D) Lava flow
Name the distinctive feature formed when basaltic lava erupts onto the ocean floor.
Describe how the silica content of a magma affects the style of volcanic eruption it produces.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for:
- High silica content produces a high viscosity magma that traps gases, leading to an explosive eruption / steeper-sided volcano
- Low silica content produces a low viscosity magma that allows gases to escape freely, leading to a passive / effusive eruption and a gently sloping shield volcano
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a geologist would distinguish between a sill and a dyke in the field, referring to their relationship with surrounding rock layers.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for:
- A sill is concordant: it runs parallel to the bedding / rock layers above and below (1 mark)
- A dyke is discordant: it cuts across the bedding / rock layers at an angle, typically near-vertical (1 mark)
- Both show baked / metamorphosed country rock at their contacts as evidence of heat from the intrusion (1 mark)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the origin and structure of columnar jointing with pillow lava, referring to the environment in which each forms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear comparison of both structures: columnar jointing forms in subaerial (surface) basaltic flows when lava cools and contracts, producing hexagonal columns perpendicular to the cooling surface; pillow lava forms when basalt erupts underwater and the outer surface quenches in cold water, forming rounded blobs. Both involve basaltic magma but in contrasting environments. Stated in a contrastive structure.
Secure: Both features described correctly; environment noted for each; limited direct comparison.
Developing: One feature described correctly; other only mentioned.
Emerging: Vague reference to lava cooling with no distinction between the two features.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how well the jelly lava flow experiment models the behaviour of real magma during volcanic eruption.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three distinct strengths and limitations evaluated with explanation. Strengths: demonstrates that higher viscosity produces steeper, shorter flows and steeper cone angles, mimicking the contrast between shield and stratovolcanoes; shows that flow distance decreases as viscosity increases; demonstrates the link between viscosity and slope angle in an accessible way. Limitations: jelly does not model temperature (real lava solidifies as it cools, changing viscosity mid-flow); jelly does not model gas behaviour (real explosive eruptions depend on gas pressure build-up); jelly cannot reproduce pyroclastic material; scale and rate are not representative. Evaluative conclusion about overall usefulness.
Secure: Two strengths and two limitations with partial explanations.
Developing: One strength and one limitation; limited explanation of mechanism.
Emerging: General statements about the experiment with no specific strengths or limitations.

knowledge_checks.q: What type of eruption produces broad, gently sloping shield volcanoes?
options: Explosive eruption from high-viscosity andesitic magma
Passive fissure or central-vent eruption from low-viscosity basaltic magma

knowledge_checks.q: Which feature distinguishes a dyke from a sill when viewed in a cliff face?
options: A dyke is always thicker than a sill
A dyke runs parallel to the bedding, a sill cuts across it
A dyke cuts across bedding, a sill runs parallel to it
A dyke is always of granite composition

knowledge_checks.q: Hexagonal columns formed in thick basalt flows by contraction during cooling are called _____ jointing.
A large, irregular deep intrusion of granite that forms the bulk of the crust is called a _____.
Match each igneous body to its key property:
right: Forms by underwater eruption of basalt

flashcard_questions.q: What controls whether a volcanic eruption is explosive or passive?
flashcard_questions.a: Magma viscosity, which is controlled mainly by silica content

flashcard_questions.q: What type of volcano does low-viscosity basaltic magma typically build?
flashcard_questions.a: A broad, gently sloping shield volcano
Lava erupting along a linear crack rather than from a single central vent

flashcard_questions.q: What causes columnar jointing in basalt?
flashcard_questions.a: Contraction of thick lava as it cools, forming hexagonal columns

flashcard_questions.q: Name a British example of columnar jointing in basalt.
What is pillow lava and where does it form?
flashcard_questions.a: Rounded basalt blobs formed when lava erupts underwater and quenches rapidly

flashcard_questions.q: Is a sill concordant or discordant with bedding?
Is a dyke concordant or discordant with bedding?

flashcard_questions.a: A zone of thermally altered country rock surrounding an igneous intrusion

flashcard_questions.q: Name a British example of exposed granite plutons.
flashcard_questions.a: Dartmoor or Bodmin Moor (part of the Cornubian batholith)

flashcard_questions.q: What relative age rule applies to a dyke cutting through sedimentary rock?
flashcard_questions.a: The dyke is younger than the rocks it cuts (cross-cutting relationships)

glossary_terms.definition: The resistance of a magma to flow; a high-viscosity magma is thick and sticky, while a low-viscosity magma is runny and flows easily.
A long crack or vent in the Earth's crust through which lava erupts along its entire length rather than from a central point.
Six-sided (hexagonal) columns that form perpendicular to cooling surfaces in thick basaltic lava flows, produced as the lava contracts during cooling.
Rounded, pillow-shaped masses of basalt formed when lava erupts underwater and the outer surface quenches rapidly.
Bodies of igneous rock that solidified from magma within the Earth's crust, never reaching the surface.
A sheet-like igneous intrusion that runs parallel to the surrounding rock layers (concordant), injected along bedding planes.
A vertical or steeply inclined sheet-like igneous intrusion that cuts across the surrounding rock layers (discordant).
A large, irregular mass of intrusive igneous rock, typically granite, that formed deep in the crust and is exposed at the surface by erosion.

items.title: Cracking the Code of Columnar Jointing (Hannah Fry)
items.description: Mathematician Hannah Fry explains why cooling lava contracts into hexagonal columns — the physics behind the Giant's Causeway.

items.title: The Bizarre Giant's Causeway Columns (GeoCurious)
items.description: GeoCurious explores the geology and formation history of the Giant's Causeway — the spec's key British example of columnar jointing.

items.title: Fire of Love (2022)
items.description: Volcanologists Katia and Maurice Krafft documented fissure eruptions, lava lakes and pyroclastic flows up close — viscosity and eruption style in real life.

items.title: Into the Inferno (Werner Herzog, 2016)
items.description: Herzog's documentary visits active volcanoes from Ethiopia to North Korea — comparing basaltic lava lakes with explosive andesitic systems.

items.title: Dante's Peak (1997)
items.description: Disaster film depicting a stratovolcano eruption — viscous andesitic magma, pyroclastic flows and lahar hazards, loosely based on Mt St Helens.

items.title: BGS — Volcanoes: Discovering Geology
items.description: British Geological Survey pages on volcano types, eruption styles and the geological evidence for ancient volcanic activity in Britain.

items.title: USGS — Volcano Hazards Program
items.description: USGS comprehensive resource on eruption styles, lava types, intrusive bodies and monitoring of active volcanoes worldwide.

items.description: Free activities including the jelly lava flow viscosity model referenced in the specification — demonstrates slope angle vs viscosity relationship.

items.description: Covers the key intrusive igneous body types with diagrams — useful for distinguishing concordant sills from discordant dykes.
